*A first foray into recognizing KV caches as a model within a model.*

Transformers are the de-facto architectural choice for large language models. 
They compute attention scores over increasingly long context lengths, which was largely been made possible by KV-caching that stores previous key and value activations.
The costs of such a linearly increasing cache size motivates research to manage cache size while maintaining expressivity.

We take another approach to this problem and instead ask if we can treat the KV cache as a trainable, fast-weight model instead of inference infrastructure.
This post will serve as the conceptual motivation for this project and explain why Titans-style neural memory is a natural choice.
The technical details will follow in part two.

## Memory Fundamentals

### Statefulness in LLMs
During autoregressive inference, the model does not recompute attention over the whole prefix from scratch.
At each decoding step, the model only needs to compute a fresh query, key, and value for the most recent token generated.
The new query vector then attends over the cached KV state.

In effect, we can store long prefixes as numerical vectors to grab from off the shelf.
For instance, an agent's preamble consisting of MCP tool specs, system prompts, and skill descriptions forms a computational *state* of dimension sequence length x hidden dimension x attention head dimension x number of model layers.

### A Model Within a Model
In more traditional language, activation matrices are really just the *fast weights* which are programmable by *slow weights*, or what we generally view to be parameters in the model [@hebb1949organization; @hinton1987fast; @schmidhuber1992learning; @ba2016using].

If we follow the LLM computation chain a step further, we can actually interpret the attention operation, $\operatorname{softmax}(qK^\top)V$, as a 2-layer MLP, where fast weight $K^T$ serves as the first layer, the softmax as the nonlinearity, and $V$ as the second layer.
Given that for any unique LLM session, most of $K^T$ and $Q$ are static and cached, **attention in modern LLMs is functionally an MLP in fast-weight space.**

This view is powerful but estranged from most mainstream tracts of LLM research.
Therefore, we ask:

1. What would it mean to treat the KV cache as a first-class citizen, and how can we bring the machinery of modern machine learning to bear on it?

2. What becomes possible when attention is no longer constrained to remember by accumulating tokens, but can instead learn, compress, rewrite, and retrieve through weights?


## Architecture overview

The first thing deep learning teaches us is that we can trade width for depth.
Titan-Llama is a first foray into recognizing KV caches as a model within a model, and specifically trading the KV cache, which are really just ultrawide fast-weight layes, with a deep architecture. 
Though it is called Titan-Llama, our vision for this is to utilize it as a tack on to any existing LLM and serve as an inference capability enabler.

Linear attention frames the matrix $K^TV$ as both a recurrent state and a mapping that transforms a query into value space--but this effectively gets rid of the nonlinearity the softmax in full attention provides.
Titans takes this view a step further and transforms the uni-matrix mapping into a multi-layer MLP, which is trained explicitly to memorize K -> V mappings at test-time.
At the same time, a forward pass is equivalent to one-shotting the output in hidden stream space without having to explicitly store K and V vectors in a linearly growing KV cache.

Fundamentally, Titans takes a hierarchical approach to long-context language modeling, where local hidden streams computed are appended to with "virtual tokens" retrieved by querying the memory.
The interesting thing to notice here is that since we are appending to the hidden stream of local attention, we are effectively training the slow weights within the Titan module to be good at RAG.
We are mapping queries from our current local attention window to values that are relevant values from before.

What if instead of tasking the NMM with a dual objective^[learning the bindings from K -> V *and* RAG], we did the opposite and instead emphasized the hierachical structure of textual dependencies. 
In effect, the outer loss would train the NMM weights to produce virtual K,V tokens that are appendable into the hidden stream, and gradient updates generated at test-time flavor these K,V output tokens.
